# The Peculiar Gift of Boredom

I've been thinking a lot lately about boredom—that strange, dull ache that settles into an afternoon when nothing much is happening and there's nowhere particular you need to be. It's an emotion we're trained to hate, to fill, to medicate against with the endless scroll of our phones and the infinite buffet of streaming content. We treat boredom like a disease, something to be cured as quickly as possible. But what if we've got it entirely wrong? What if boredom is actually one of the most underrated gifts we can give ourselves?

I came to this realization on an ordinary Tuesday in October. The weather was the kind that doesn't announce itself—not beautiful, not terrible, just present. I had blocked out the afternoon intending to do something productive, but a combination of circumstances conspired against efficiency: my internet was spotty, I was tired from travel the previous week, and I'd left my good notebook at my partner's apartment. I sat in my living room surrounded by the minor frustrations of modern life, and I found myself completely unable to access the usual escape routes. No streaming services worked well enough to hold my attention. Books felt like too much commitment. I was too restless to nap.

So I did something radical: I let myself be bored.

I sat on the couch and watched dust motes float through the afternoon light. I thought about a conversation I'd had three weeks earlier with someone I cared about—a conversation where I'd said something I wasn't entirely proud of. Not anything catastrophic, just thoughtless. I'd been carrying it around without quite realizing it, like a pebble in my shoe that you stop noticing until you finally stop and take it out. Sitting there in that boredom, the thought surfaced and I actually *felt* it instead of performing the usual mental gymnastics to avoid it.

I thought about that and decided I would reach out and apologize, properly, not in that performative way where you're apologizing while checking your phone. I would do it tomorrow.

Then I thought about my work, about a project I'd been struggling with for months. In that bored state, untethered from the constant stimulation my brain had learned to expect, something shifted. I saw the problem from a different angle—not because I was actively trying to solve it, but because my mind had space to wander, to make unexpected connections, to be genuinely creative in the way that requires some fallow time.

I remember reading something once about how the most innovative companies started protecting "boredom time" for their employees after they realized that some of their best ideas came not during intense brainstorming sessions but during the periods of seemingly unproductive wandering. Google's famous "20% time" was built on this principle—space for minds to roam. The best creative people I know aren't the ones constantly optimizing every minute of their day. They're the ones who seem to have pockets of unscheduled time where thinking happens almost accidentally.

We've become so efficient at avoiding boredom that we've forgotten why it exists in the first place. Boredom is a signal. It's not punishment; it's information. It's your mind and body telling you that the current stimulus level doesn't match what you need. Sometimes that signal is pointing you toward something you need to pay attention to—something you're avoiding, or something that deserves more of your focused time. Sometimes it's simply pointing you toward a need to rest and reset.

But here's what's tricky: you can't hack boredom. You can't use it as a productivity tool while simultaneously trying to optimize around it. The moment you sit down to be bored "for the sake of creativity," you've lost it. True boredom is unintentional. It's the accidental open space where something unexpected can grow.

I think about my grandmother, who lived a long life and seemed genuinely at peace with it most of the time. She had her routines—her morning coffee, her garden, her correspondence with friends. But she also seemed to have no problem with empty time. She would sit on her porch and look at trees. She would reorganize the same drawer multiple times. She knitted, not because she needed the output but because the repetitive motion seemed to suit her. If you asked her what she was doing during those stretches of time, she would probably have looked confused by the question. She was just... being.

There was something I envied about that, though I wouldn't have had the language for it when I was younger. Now I wonder if the increasing rate of anxiety and depression in our culture isn't partly connected to our complete eradication of empty time. We're never bored, yes, but we're also never truly at rest. Our brains never get to the state where they can genuinely process and integrate experience. We're all accumulating undigested emotional and intellectual material, scrolling past it while we pretend to be entertained.

The pandemic offered everyone an accidental gift of boredom, and I watched how people responded to it with real terror. The first few days of lockdown, people still had that novelty and shock to sustain them. But after the first week or two, once it became clear this was the new normal for a while, the panic became visible. Suddenly everyone needed hobbies. Everyone was sourdough baking and starting home gyms and taking online courses. We couldn't just be bored together; we had to optimize the boredom, turn it into productive self-improvement.

I'm not saying there's anything wrong with sourdough or online courses. But I do think it's telling that so few people's first instinct was simply to sit with the strangeness and emptiness of it. To feel bored and let that feeling teach them something. Most of us grabbed at distractions as fast as we could manage.

There's also something about boredom that's become countercultural in a way that feels almost radical. In a world where productivity is conflated with worth, boredom is a kind of rebellion. Choosing to be unoccupied, unoptimized, unplugged—there's something almost subversive about it. It's a refusal to participate in the constant quantification of time into billable hours or content consumption or self-improvement metrics.

I've noticed that the people I know who seem the most genuinely content aren't the ones who've successfully gamified every aspect of their lives or built the most impressive hustle portfolios. They're the ones who seem to have made peace with the fact that large portions of their time won't be documented, won't be productive, won't be Instagram-worthy. They're boring, in the best sense. They live unexceptional lives and they seem to find them satisfactory.

Maybe that's the real secret that boredom holds: it's where you discover the difference between the life you're supposed to want and the life you actually want. All the constant stimulation and optimization keeps you pointed in whatever direction the world thinks you should go. But boredom, if you let yourself sit in it long enough, might point you back toward yourself. It might tell you that the thing you're working toward doesn't actually matter to you. Or it might tell you the opposite—that you want something so badly you've been afraid to admit it because it doesn't fit the narrative you've constructed.

I wonder sometimes what I would discover if I let myself be bored more systematically. Not just that accidental Tuesday afternoon, but as an actual practice. I think I'm afraid of what I might find. It's easier to keep moving, to fill the spaces, to stay perpetually stimulated and distracted. Boredom asks you to be still, and stillness can be uncomfortable. It requires you to actually inhabit your own life rather than watching it happen from the outside.

The irony is that our culture is obsessed with authenticity and living our best lives, and yet we've engineered authenticity and genuine living out of possibility by refusing to let ourselves experience the empty, uncomfortable spaces where actual personhood develops. Authenticity can't be a purchased product, but we keep trying to buy it. We think if we just consume the right things, optimize the right systems, follow the right people, we'll somehow stumble into an authentic version of ourselves. Meanwhile, the actual path to authenticity runs through the uncomfortable boredom of facing ourselves without distraction.

I'm trying to be more intentional about building boredom into my days now, though I'm admittedly not very good at it yet. It goes against every instinct I've developed over decades of exposure to stimulation and productivity culture. I'm trying to have a cup of coffee in the morning without immediately reaching for my phone. I'm trying to take walks where I deliberately don't listen to podcasts or music. I'm trying to sit with my own thoughts and let them meander wherever they want to go.

It's awkward. My mind rebels. I feel the itch to check in on the world, to see what I'm missing, to accomplish something with this time. But I'm discovering that if I can sit with that discomfort for ten minutes or so, something shifts. The panic settles. My breath deepens. I start noticing things—the particular quality of light on a familiar street, the way my own thoughts actually work when I'm not drowning them out, what I actually feel about my life rather than what I think I should feel.

And here's the thing I didn't expect: it's not actually unpleasant once you get past the initial resistance. There's something almost luxurious about it, about giving yourself permission to take up space without accomplishing anything. In a world where every moment is supposed to be monetized or optimized or turned into content, the simple act of wasting time becomes oddly radical and genuinely restful.

I think boredom is where you remember that you're alive. Not living the life you're supposed to live, not performing the self you think you should be, but just... existing in your own experience. I think we need more of it. I think our children need more of it—bored children actually playing instead of being continuously entertained. I think our workers need more of it. I think our artists especially need more of it.

The gift of boredom is the gift of your own mind back. It's the gift of possibility, of genuine creativity rather than optimization, of authenticity rather than performance. It's boring, literally, but that might be exactly why it matters. In a world addicted to novelty and stimulation and excitement, boredom is the last frontier of genuine peace. So maybe I'll sit here a little longer and let it teach me whatever it has to teach. Maybe I'll let myself be productively unproductive. Maybe I'll be boring enough to become real.
